title: Enums and flags
sub: A struct over an integer, baked-in values, undefined values, [Flags] and HasFlag
cards/0/title: To the CLR an enum is a struct over an integer
cards/0/body:
An enumeration (enum) is a value type derived from System.Enum. It has exactly one instance field — value__ of the underlying integer type (int by default). The member names are constants: static literal fields holding a number.

So a Color variable takes as much space as its underlying type, and in machine code it is just a number. You can pick the underlying type: byte, short, long and their unsigned pairs.
cards/0/deep:
Since it is a plain integer inside, a boxed enum unboxes into its underlying type and back: (int)(object)DayOfWeek.Monday works — we saw this in the unit "How a type is built". Methods like ToString are declared in System.Enum, which is a reference type, so calling them on an enum value usually requires boxing.

The constraint where T : struct, Enum is available since C# 7.3; the generic APIs are built on it: Enum.Parse<T>, Enum.GetValues<T>() (.NET 5).
cards/1/q: enum Color { Red, Green, Blue }. What does Color c = (Color)42; do?
cards/1/options/0: Compiles and runs: c holds the number 42
cards/1/options/3: Runs, and c ends up as Blue
cards/1/explain: Casting an integer to an enum just changes the type of the number. The CLR does not check whether such a member exists. c.ToString() returns "42".
cards/1/wrong/1: There is no check on the cast: an enum is the same integer.
cards/1/wrong/3: The value is not clamped to the nearest member; it stays 42.
cards/2/title: Values are baked into the calling code
cards/2/body:
An enum member is a constant. When the app writes Status.Blocked, the compiler puts a number into its IL, not a reference to the field. After the build the app does not know the name, only 1.

The "version 2" scenario: the library inserted a new member at the start, and all implicit numbers shifted. An app built against the old version keeps comparing with the old numbers — which now mean something else. No load error, just a silently wrong result.

Rules for public enums: set values explicitly, add new members at the end, never renumber or remove old ones.
cards/3/q: The library was updated to v2 from the card above, and the app was not rebuilt. What does its check if (user.Status == Status.Blocked) do?
cards/3/options/0: Compares with 1 and treats active users as blocked
cards/3/options/1: Compares with Blocked by name and works correctly
cards/3/explain: The app's IL holds the number 1 — the value of Blocked at build time. In v2 one means Active. Nobody looks the field up by name, so there is no exception either.
cards/3/wrong/2: MissingFieldException can happen when code accesses a field. The compiler has already substituted the constant as a number.
cards/4/body:
An enum variable can hold any number: from a cast, a database, JSON, or default. Details that matter:

  • default(Color) and uninitialized fields are always 0, even if there is no member with value 0. That is why the first member is usually None or Unknown = 0.
  • Enum.TryParse<Color>("42", out c) returns true: a numeric string parses into the number whether or not such a member exists.
  • Enum.IsDefined(c) checks whether there is a member with exactly that value.
  • A switch statement without default simply skips an unknown value. A switch expression that lists every name produces warning CS8524 and throws SwitchExpressionException on an unknown value.
cards/4/deep:
Why the compiler wants a _ arm even though every name is listed: to it, Light is the whole int range, and the names are just a few points in it. The separate warning CS8524 (rather than the usual CS8509) is specifically about unnamed values — so you can suppress it if the input is definitely validated.

Enum.IsDefined in .NET 5+ has a generic form IsDefined<T>(T) without boxing; the runtime caches member values, but it is still a lookup, not a single comparison. On a hot path the range check is written by hand: (uint)l <= (uint)Light.Green, if the values are contiguous.
cards/5/q: enum Color { Red = 1, Green = 2 }. What is true? Select all.
cards/5/options/0: Enum.TryParse<Color>("42", out var c) returns true
cards/5/options/2: default(Color) is 0 even though there is no such member
cards/5/options/4: A switch expression with arms for Red and Green and no _ gives a warning
cards/5/explain: Casting to an enum checks nothing — that is exactly why IsDefined and the _ arm exist. TryParse accepts any numeric string that fits the underlying type.
cards/6/body:
A flags enum is one where every member is a separate bit: values 1, 2, 4, 8… Combinations are built with |, tested with &, cleared with & ~.

The [Flags] attribute does not assign powers of two — you write them yourself; otherwise for None, Read, Write, Exec implicit numbering gives 0, 1, 2, 3, and Read | Write collides with Exec. The attribute changes only the text form: ToString prints the combination by names, and Enum.Parse understands "Read, Write".
cards/6/deep: If a number cannot be fully decomposed into defined flags, ToString prints it as digits: for (Perm)9 — "9". Handy combinations can be declared as members: ReadWrite = Read | Write; ToString will prefer that name. Up to 64 flags fit into long/ulong; beyond that you need a BitArray or your own struct.
cards/7/q: The [Flags] attribute was removed from Perm, the values stayed. What does Console.WriteLine(Perm.Read | Perm.Write) print?
cards/7/explain: Without [Flags], ToString looks for a member with exactly the value 3, finds none and prints the number. The bitwise operations themselves work the same with or without the attribute.
cards/8/body:
The signature is bool HasFlag(Enum flag). The parameter type is System.Enum, a reference type, so the argument is boxed. The method itself is declared in System.Enum, so the value it is called on is boxed too. Inside there is also a check that the types match, otherwise ArgumentException.

In .NET Framework each call cost two allocations, and hot code replaced it with (p & f) == f. Since .NET Core 2.1 the JIT recognizes HasFlag as an intrinsic and emits the same bitwise comparison — no boxing.

The logical trap remains: p.HasFlag(Perm.None) is always true — every number "contains" zero bits.
cards/8/deep: The optimization kicks in when the JIT sees both types exactly. In code where the value already sits in an Enum or object, the boxing has already happened earlier, and there is no miracle. One more subtlety: Enum.IsDefined returns false for a flag combination unless that combination is declared as its own member — you cannot validate flags with IsDefined.
cards/9/q: Which of the variables b–e gets true?
cards/9/explain: HasFlag(None) checks (p & 0) == 0 — always true. p has neither Write nor Exec, and the value 3 is not declared as a member, so IsDefined returns false.
cards/10/title: Cost: where an enum costs money
cards/10/body:
Comparisons, switch, bitwise operations — free: it is integer work. The JIT often turns a switch over dense values into a jump table.

You pay where a name or reflection is involved:

  • ToString() and interpolation — a name lookup by value (the runtime caches the names and returns the ready string for a declared member, but the call through System.Enum usually costs a boxing, and for flag combinations and unknown values a new string is built);
  • Enum.Parse, GetNames, GetValues — string parsing and new arrays on every call;
  • non-generic APIs (Enum.IsDefined(typeof(T), value), HasFlag before .NET Core 2.1) — boxing.

If names are needed on a hot path (logs, JSON), people write their own switch with string literals or a cached array of names.
cards/10/deep: Serializers solve it the same way: System.Text.Json with JsonStringEnumConverter caches the names, and its source generator emits code without reflection. For Native AOT the generic Enum.GetValues<T>() is preferable to the Type-based versions: the non-generic GetValues(Type) creates an array of a type the AOT compiler may not have prepared, and it is annotated with a warning.
cards/11/q: Complete a generic check that a value is a declared enum member
cards/11/explain: The struct, Enum constraint (C# 7.3) admits only enums. Enum.IsDefined<T>(T) from .NET 5 works without boxing and without typeof.
